newsitem.title: USA: Chicago Fed denies policy confidentiality breach.
newsitem.headline: Chicago Fed denies policy confidentiality breach.

text.p: The Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago said on Wednesday the presence of a consultant at two meetings involving monetary policy discussions at the bank did not result in any breach of confidentiality.
"There was no breach of confidentiality," the Chicago Fed said in a statement.

The statement was issued following a letter by House Banking Committee Ranking Democrat Henry Gonzalez (D-Tx.) to Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan requesting information about two monetary policy meetings at the Chicago Fed.

The Chicago Fed said the meetings involved a "consultant who, as part of a temporary assignment, attended two briefings, one on January 9, 1997, and the other on February 3, 1997, and who was bound by a strict confidentiality agreement."
Martin Eichenbaum, Professor of Economics at Northwestern University, told Reuters he was the consultant who attended the two briefings.
"I have an ongoing relationship as a consultant with the Chicago Fed that dates back a number of years," Eichenbaum, whose field of expertise is monetary policy, said.
"I signed a confidentiality statement," Eichenbaum added. "There was some ambiguity about the precise meetings a consultant should and shoult not attend."
The Chicago Fed also said it has "taken steps to assure that only employees with specific clearance will participate" in monetary policy briefings.

In his April 2 letter, Gonzalez requested Greenspan to "provide ... names, dates and details of all persons who were not Federal Reserve employees who have attended such meetings at any of these banks, the Board of Governors or the Federal Open Market Committee meetings within the last three years."
Gonzalez's query into the Chicago Fed operations began with a two-page memo dated January 14, addressed to William Gram, Secretary and General Counsel at the Chicago Fed.

The memo, whose content Reuters obtained and first reported about on February 13, asked the Chicago Fed to specifiy the role of consultants at the bank, as well as salaries of top-paid employees, and the breakdown of employees "by race, sex, disability and age."
Both Gonzalez's office and the Chicago Fed said anonymous letters prompted the inquiry. A Chicago Fed source said the letters were likely sent by a disgruntled employee.
The Fed System, including the Chicago Fed, is currently downsizing some of its oeprations due to new technology and banking regulations.

Chicago Fed President Michael Moskow, in a March 7 letter to Gonzalez that was made available to Reuters, said he and the bank's research director invited Eichenbaum to attend two meetings because the bank "recently lost two macro-economists and we wanted to use Mr. Eichenbaum to fill this gap."
The 12 Fed district bank presidents attend FOMC meetings, though only five of them vote at any given time. They consult with their staff in the days preceeding FOMC meetings.

Moskow's March 7 letter acknowledged that, after Counsel Gram advised him "on the rules governing these briefings," "I immediately decided that Mr. Eichenbaum should not attend such briefings in the future."

According to Moskow, the February 3 meeting -- one day before the February 4-5 FOMC meeting -- discussed economic data contained in the "Green Book" the Fed uses for policy deliberations, while the January 9 meeting involved "a discount rate briefing."
In September 1996, a senior Fed source told Reuters eight out of 12 Fed banks wanted a discount rate hike.
The Fed recently confirmed Reuters' report that prompted an internal Fed investigation, supported by the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

Gonzalez stressed the Fed must be watchful about the disclosure of sensitive information "such as a non-public discount rate decision, which is inside information that can be exploited for huge profits before it is made public."
Gonzalez also urged Greenspan to release the full transcripts of FOMC meetings "in a timely manner," and requested an answer to his letter by April 16.
